source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating continuous batching. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Runbook: record model/version, tokenizer, precision, hardware, software, prompt/output-length distributions, offered load, concurrency, batching policy, cache state, and warm-up. Continuous batching admits new sequences and retires completed ones at iteration boundaries, reusing active slots and KV blocks instead of waiting for a fixed batch to finish. Check admission delay, active batch size, KV fragmentation, queueing, HBM capacity, and scheduler fairness. Boundary condition: gains can disappear or tails can worsen under low load, bursty traffic, long-request mixtures, padding, scheduler overhead, or memory pressure. Compare with a matched static-batch control and measure TTFT, inter-token p50/p95/p99, tokens/s, memory, evictions/OOMs, and errors.
risks: Length mix, offered load, scheduler overhead, and padding can change throughput and tail latency.
KV fragmentation or admission mistakes can cause memory exhaustion, starvation, or unfairness.
Incorrect request or cache isolation can produce wrong outputs or cross-tenant leakage.
evidence_required: Matched static-batch and continuous-batching trials across light, saturated, bursty, and representative length regimes.
Report TTFT and inter-token p50/p95/p99, tokens/s with units, queueing, active batch size, KV/HBM use, evictions/OOMs, and errors.
Verify correctness, fairness, isolation, and predefined rollback thresholds before rollout.

source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating continuous batching. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Investigate continuous batching by fixing model, tokenizer, precision, hardware, software, request lengths, offered load, concurrency, cache policy, and warm-up. Mechanism: the scheduler admits waiting sequences and removes completed sequences at iteration boundaries, so active slots and KV blocks can be reused without waiting for the longest request in a static batch. Inspect admission/retirement timing, active batch size, padding, queueing, KV fragmentation, memory bandwidth, evictions, and fairness. Boundary condition: high utilization is not sufficient evidence of benefit; long or bursty requests, scheduler overhead, and memory limits may improve aggregate tokens/s while degrading p99 latency. Use a matched control and predefined SLO/rollback gates.
risks: Length heterogeneity and queueing can increase tail latency despite higher occupancy.
KV fragmentation, paging, or admission bugs can cause OOMs, stalls, or starvation.
Shared batching must preserve request, adapter, and tenant isolation.
evidence_required: Run matched controls with identical request traces, limits, and warm-up across multiple load regimes.
Collect latency percentiles, throughput, queueing/admission delay, active batch size, fragmentation, memory, eviction/OOM, and error rates.
Confirm output correctness, fairness, isolation, and rollback criteria.

source_user: Explain how tensor parallelism interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Tensor parallelism shards computation within layers and introduces collective communication; the best degree depends on memory, topology, batch, and communication cost.
corrected_answer: Tensor parallelism shards layer weights and intermediate computation across devices; a mechanism such as a sharded matrix multiply followed by an all-reduce or all-gather exchanges partial results before the next operation. Sharding can reduce per-device weight memory and enable a model to fit, and may improve throughput when compute is distributed, but collectives add synchronization, bandwidth, and launch overhead to latency. Boundary condition: increasing the degree is not monotonically better; topology, message size, batch/sequence shape, precision, load balance, and interconnect determine whether communication dominates. State these assumptions and measure end-to-end and per-token latency, throughput, device memory, collective time, and tail behavior against a matched degree-1 or alternative control.
risks: Collective synchronization and topology mismatch can erase compute or memory benefits and raise tails.
Uneven sharding, stragglers, or failures can stall the whole group.
Incorrect rank/device mapping or communication configuration can cause wrong results or unavailable service.
evidence_required: Benchmark identical model, precision, sequence lengths, batch/concurrency, and software across tensor-parallel degrees.
Report TTFT/inter-token p50/p95/p99, throughput with units, per-device memory, utilization, collective bytes/time, and failure rates.
Verify numerical correctness, rank isolation, timeout handling, and rollback thresholds.

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether tensor parallelism helps a serving workload. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Tensor parallelism shards computation within layers and introduces collective communication; the best degree depends on memory, topology, batch, and communication cost.
corrected_answer: Hypothesis: for a specified model and workload, tensor parallel degree d meets a stated latency or throughput target and memory budget relative to a matched control without unacceptable failure or tail regressions. Hold model/version, tokenizer, precision, prompt/output lengths, concurrency, batching, hardware topology, software, warm-up, and request trace constant; vary only d where feasible. Mechanism to observe: sharded layer computation requires collectives such as all-reduce/all-gather, whose time and synchronization may overlap or compete with compute. Measure TTFT, inter-token and completion p50/p95/p99, requests/s and tokens/s, per-device memory/utilization, collective time/bytes, queueing, errors, and power if relevant. Boundary condition: results depend on message size and interconnect; test light, saturated, and representative loads, and roll back on predefined SLO, correctness, or capacity failures.
risks: A single batch or topology can misrepresent communication-dominated production behavior.
Collective time, stragglers, and rank failures can inflate tails or cause group-wide outages.
Configuration changes can affect numerical correctness and isolation.
evidence_required: Use randomized or repeated matched trials across tensor degrees, topologies, load levels, and representative length mixes.
Report latency percentiles, throughput units, memory headroom, collective timing, queueing, errors, and confidence intervals where appropriate.
Predefine correctness, SLO, capacity, and rollback gates before evaluation.

source_user: What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about tensor parallelism? Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Tensor parallelism shards computation within layers and introduces collective communication; the best degree depends on memory, topology, batch, and communication cost.
corrected_answer: State at least: model architecture and parameter/KV sizes; tensor-parallel degree and rank placement; GPU type, count, topology, interconnect, and available bandwidth; precision and kernels; software and collective versions; prompt/output lengths, batch/concurrency, request mix, cache state, offered load, and warm-up; baseline degree and metric definitions. Mechanism: each layer combines sharded partial results through collectives, so communication and synchronization are part of the critical path. Boundary condition: a degree that lowers per-device memory may hurt latency or throughput when messages are small, topology is poor, batch is low, or collectives dominate. Distinguish measured results from estimates, report units and percentiles, and do not generalize across hardware or workloads without matched evidence.
risks: Unstated topology, workload, or baseline makes comparisons non-reproducible and potentially misleading.
Communication and synchronization can create tail latency, bottlenecks, or group-wide failure.
Rank placement and version mismatches can cause hangs or incorrect results.
evidence_required: Record full hardware, topology, software, model, precision, and workload configuration.
Measure matched baselines with latency/throughput units, memory headroom, collective time, tails, and error rates.
Validate claims across relevant degrees and representative load before deployment.

source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating tensor parallelism. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Tensor parallelism shards computation within layers and introduces collective communication; the best degree depends on memory, topology, batch, and communication cost.
corrected_answer: Runbook: capture model/version, precision, tensor-parallel degree, rank-to-device mapping, topology, interconnect, kernels, collective library, sequence lengths, batch/concurrency, cache state, and warm-up. Verify outputs against a trusted single-device or equivalent reference. Mechanism: inspect sharded layer kernels and the all-reduce/all-gather operations that synchronize partial results; correlate their time and bytes with end-to-end latency. Check memory headroom, utilization, queueing, stragglers, retries, and collective timeouts. Boundary condition: communication may dominate at low batch, small messages, or cross-socket/cross-node placement even when sharding reduces memory. Measure TTFT, inter-token p50/p95/p99, tokens/s, per-device memory, collective metrics, and errors; stop on correctness, isolation, or SLO violations.
risks: Bad rank mapping or topology can cause severe performance loss or collective hangs.
A failed or straggling rank can block the entire inference group.
Reference mismatches, stale binaries, or unsafe diagnostics can hide correctness or security issues.
evidence_required: Reproduce with recorded topology and configuration and compare to a trusted reference.
Report percentile latency, throughput units, memory headroom, collective time/bytes, timeout and error rates.
Use least-privilege diagnostics and predefined stop/rollback criteria.

source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating tensor parallelism. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Tensor parallelism shards computation within layers and introduces collective communication; the best degree depends on memory, topology, batch, and communication cost.
corrected_answer: Investigate by recording the model, precision, tensor-parallel degree, device/rank placement, topology, interconnect, software, lengths, batch/concurrency, cache policy, and warm-up. Mechanism: partitioned layer computation produces partial outputs that must be synchronized with collectives; profile collective duration, payload, overlap, and idle gaps alongside kernels. Compare output logits or agreed tolerances with a reference, then inspect memory headroom, load balance, queueing, retries, and timeouts. Boundary condition: higher parallelism can fit a model yet worsen latency when communication or synchronization dominates, especially with small batches, small messages, or a slow link. Report TTFT/inter-token tails, tokens/s, memory, collective metrics, and errors under a production-like load; stop for correctness, isolation, or SLO regressions.
risks: Topology and rank-placement errors can cause bottlenecks or hangs.
Group-wide synchronization magnifies stragglers and device failures.
Unverified numerical differences or diagnostics can cause incorrect service behavior or expose sensitive data.
evidence_required: Use a trusted reference and test representative degrees, topologies, batch sizes, and loads.
Capture percentile latency, throughput, memory, collective payload/time, queueing, timeout, and error metrics.
Apply access-controlled profiling, correctness checks, and rollback gates.

source_user: Explain how pipeline parallelism interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Pipeline parallelism partitions layers across stages and can require microbatching to reduce pipeline bubbles.
corrected_answer: Pipeline parallelism partitions consecutive layers across stages, so activations move between devices and each stage processes a microbatch before forwarding it. A concrete mechanism is overlapping microbatches through the stages; without enough microbatches, fill and drain create pipeline bubbles and idle capacity. It can reduce per-device weight memory and enable larger models, while adding activation communication, scheduling, and often training-specific memory costs; for autoregressive serving, stage synchronization can affect each token's latency. Boundary condition: more microbatches can raise throughput after fill, but may increase latency, activation memory, or queueing and cannot remove imbalance between stages. Measure stage utilization, bubble fraction, activation memory, communication, TTFT/inter-token latency, throughput, and p95/p99 under stated workload assumptions.
risks: Uneven layer partitioning or straggler stages can dominate end-to-end latency.
Activation buffering and microbatching can exhaust memory or increase queueing and tails.
Stage or communication failures can stall the pipeline and risk partial/inconsistent work.
evidence_required: Benchmark matched stage partitions and microbatch counts with fixed model, hardware, lengths, and load.
Report throughput units, TTFT/inter-token p50/p95/p99, stage utilization, bubble fraction, activation memory, communication, and errors.
Verify numerical correctness, bounded memory, failure recovery, and rollback criteria.

source_user: What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about pipeline parallelism? Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Pipeline parallelism partitions layers across stages and can require microbatching to reduce pipeline bubbles.
corrected_answer: State model and layer-to-stage partition, device types and topology, precision and kernels, communication path and bandwidth, pipeline schedule, microbatch count and sizes, sequence lengths, batch/concurrency, cache state, offered load, warm-up, and whether the claim concerns training or serving. Mechanism: stages forward activations between devices and overlap microbatches; fill/drain and stage imbalance create bubbles that reduce useful utilization. Boundary condition: a higher microbatch count may increase aggregate throughput but also activation memory, queueing, and per-request latency, while a small batch may leave stages idle. Compare against an explicit non-pipelined or alternative parallel baseline, report units and percentiles, and separate measured facts from estimates rather than generalizing across workloads.
risks: Claims are sensitive to stage balance, schedule, microbatching, topology, and whether workload is training or serving.
Activation memory, bubbles, or communication can negate apparent scaling.
Stage failures or mismatched assumptions can cause stalls or incorrect results.
evidence_required: Document stage mapping, schedule, microbatching, hardware, software, and workload precisely.
Measure matched baselines with throughput units, latency percentiles, stage utilization, bubble fraction, memory, communication, and errors.
Validate correctness, recovery behavior, and capacity/rollback limits across relevant loads.

source_user: Explain how MoE interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: A mixture-of-experts model routes each token to a selected top-k set of expert feed-forward networks, so only those experts perform the expert computation while shared layers and the router still run. Mechanism: token dispatch and combine may require an all-to-all exchange across devices, and expert capacity limits can cause padding, rerouting, or dropped/overflow tokens. Sparse activation can reduce active compute or increase throughput, but routing and communication add latency and expert weights still consume distributed memory. Boundary condition: benefits depend on token-to-expert balance, top-k, capacity factor, batch, topology, and offered load; skew can make one expert the bottleneck or cause quality loss from drops. Measure routing entropy/load, dropped or padded tokens, collective time, per-expert utilization, memory, throughput, latency tails, and output quality under matched workloads.
risks: Skewed routing can overload experts, increase all-to-all traffic, and create tail latency.
Capacity overflow, token dropping, or rerouting can change model quality and correctness.
Distributed expert state and communication require isolation, failure handling, and sufficient memory.
evidence_required: Run matched dense or alternative-MoE controls over representative token mixes, batch/concurrency, loads, and top-k/capacity settings.
Report latency and throughput units, p50/p95/p99, per-expert load, routing/drop/padding rates, collective time, memory, errors, and quality metrics.
Predefine quality, SLO, capacity, and rollback gates; verify behavior under skew and device failure.
